3.text: as in earlier times, from each man one fox, mostly red, but sometimes also

5.text: seems that in the beginning the Chukchee, in their eagerness for trade, were

7.text: Thus, the tale about the opening of the Anui fair, cited before, continues

8.text: as follows: “The officer from the Czarina said again, ‘My heart is angry.

14.text: been mentioned several times; and probably it reflects knowledge of the more

15.text: recent measures carried out by Maydell. Still most of it refers to an earlier

16.text: time. The Russians certainly could have succeeded in exacting some kind of

17.text: trade-tax, to be collected at the fair. Instead of that, they tried to introduce

18.text: again tribute by subjection, the same as that which led to all the earlier wars.

19.text: This tribute was paid very irregularly, — one year (1835) by twenty-seven

20.text: men, another year (1837) by twenty men, and still another year (1838) by

21.text: only eight. And with the presents of the Government the paying of tribute

22.text: soon became quite similar to traffic. The Chukchee wanted to get the most

23.text: possible, the Russian officer wanted to give less, and thus haggling over the

24.text: tribute ensued. Still, in most cases the present given represented the current

25.text: price of the furs brought for tribute. Thus in 1806 the Chukchee tribute was

26.text: ten red foxes; as an equivalent in presents, 27 pounds of tobacco, valued at

27.text: 40.5 rubles, were given. The Governor of the Yakutsk Province, however,

28.text: was displeased with the transaction, because the value of the foxes was equal

29.text: to the value of the tobacco, plus transportation. In 1832, for each red fox,

30.text: three pounds of tobacco and an iron spear-head were given, which was still

31.text: less favorable for the Russians. In 1837, for each red fox, two pounds and

32.text: a half of tobacco, a large knife, some beads, needles, also candy, hard tack,

36.text: black foxes on the part of seven different men. In 1814 there were presented

37.text: to the Czar by the Chukchee seventy puds of walrus-ivory and seventeen

38.text: puds of peltries. This last present is uncommonly large. I presume that it

39.text: was simply the result of traffic carried on by officials with Government property
